name: Nilavilakku — the Kerala Standing Lamp
tagline: The brass lamp lit at dusk in every Kerala home and at the start of every ceremony
summary: Nilavilakku, Kerala's brass standing lamp: its history and meaning, where to see temple lamps, and where to buy an authentic hand-cast piece.
description: The nilavilakku is the tall brass oil lamp of Kerala, usually with a flared base, a slender shaft and a tiered bowl holding five wicks. It is lit at dawn and dusk in homes, and at the opening of weddings, school functions, art performances and official events.
Related forms include the hanging thookkuvilakku, the lamp column (deepasthambham) in temple courtyards and the gajalakshmi vilakku, topped with a figure of Lakshmi flanked by elephants.

history.significance: A daily symbol of light, auspiciousness and hospitality, and the most recognisable household object of Kerala culture.

timeline.event: Oil lamps feature in Indian ritual from early times; metal lamps appear in temple worship across South India.
Temples develop elaborate lamp columns and rows of lamps, such as the chuttuvilakku, lit for festivals.
The nilavilakku becomes the standard emblem of lamp-lighting at inaugurations and a popular gift and home decor item.

keyFacts: Kerala lamps are usually cast in brass or bell metal; centres such as Mannar and Aranmula are known for metalwork (verify current workshops).
The lamp is traditionally lit at sandhya (dusk), often with evening prayers.
At ceremonies, guests light the wicks one by one in turn.
Padmanabhaswamy Temple holds the Lakshadeepam, a festival of one hundred thousand lamps, once in six years.

folklore.title: The Lamp as Lakshmi
story: Households describe the lit lamp as the presence of Lakshmi, goddess of prosperity, who is invited into the home at dusk. A familiar evening prayer salutes the lamp as the supreme light that removes darkness.
Elders say the lamp should be kept clean, never left dark at nightfall, and lit by a person who has bathed. The belief shapes the daily rhythm of many Kerala homes.
folklore.note: Retold from household tradition; practices vary between families and communities.

spiritual.summary: The lamp turns the start of any task into a small ritual of attention and gratitude.

experiences.title: Dusk in a Kerala home
experiences.text: If invited to a family home at sandhya, watch the lamp being lit and stay quiet through the evening prayer.

experiences.title: Lamp-lighting at a ceremony
experiences.text: At a cultural programme you may be invited to light a wick; do it in turn, with a short pause, as hosts do.

spiritual.bestFor: Anyone interested in daily ritual and craftsmanship.
mindfulTips: Do not use the lamp as decoration without understanding its household role.
Do not step over or point your feet at a lit lamp.
Ask before photographing a family prayer.

highlights: Standing, hanging and temple lamp forms

visitorInfo.bestTime: October to March for craft-village visits; temple lamp festivals follow the temple calendar.
visitorInfo.howToReach: See and buy in Thiruvananthapuram, Kochi and Kozhikode; workshops are at Mannar (Alappuzha) and Aranmula (Pathanamthitta).
etiquette: Do not haggle for a ritual lamp in a temple precinct.
Ask about oil, wicks and cleaning before you buy.

heritage.materials: Brass or bell metal; sometimes copper or silver for gifts

whereToSee.name: Padmanabhaswamy Temple, Thiruvananthapuram
whereToSee.note: Lamps lit at festivals; Lakshadeepam every six years (check dates).

whereToSee.name: Guruvayur Sri Krishna Temple
whereToSee.note: Famed for the chuttuvilakku, a circle of lamps lit on festival evenings.

whereToBuy.name: Kairali — Kerala State Handicrafts Apex Co-operative Society emporiums
whereToBuy.note: Government-linked craft emporiums in major towns; fixed prices and craft-certified items.

whereToBuy.name: Surabhi — Handicrafts Development Corporation of Kerala emporiums
whereToBuy.note: State-run emporiums selling metalcraft, wood carving, coir and handloom; good for fixed-price first purchases.

whereToBuy.name: Mannar bell-metal workshops
whereToBuy.note: Traditional metal-casting town; visit with a local guide and ask to see casting.

experiences.name: Kerala Folklore Museum, Thripunithura
experiences.note: Private museum housed in a building assembled from traditional timber architecture; displays household objects, lamps and ritual items.

experiences.name: Sargaalaya — Kerala Arts and Crafts Village, Iringal
experiences.note: Craft village near Vadakara where artisans work and sell; allow half a day.

buyingTips: Hand-cast pieces show faint casting marks; machine-spun lamps are perfectly uniform.
Ask whether it is brass or lacquered; solid brass is heavy for its size.
Buy a matching lamp stand and keep the oil bowl clean.
Keep the receipt for customs if you are flying out of India.
